description:
FlightPowers one-way fare search: live prices read from Google Flights. Input: origin and destination IATA codes -- the destination may be several codes, as "BCN,LIS,ATH" or ["BCN","LIS","ATH"] -- plus either one departure date or a date range. Returns each flight's price, airline, duration, stops, a bookable buy_link, and Google's historical price range (price_insights_low / price_insights_high), the band that shows whether a fare is actually a good deal.

Suited to any one-way fare question, including open-ended ones. One call accepts a date range and several destinations and searches every combination: 'Cheapest flight to Sri Lanka anywhere in October' is one call, not thirty. That holds with the caller's own key. On the free sign-in allowance (10 searches a day, one per combination) a grid larger than what is left today is refused before anything runs; a grid within what is left runs, and a whole-month scan needs the caller's own key.

Each date/destination combination is one search; the count comes back in `api_usage`.

`by_destination` carries one entry per requested destination -- empty ones included, each with a `reason` that separates a destination with no flights from one that was not searched, whose search failed, or whose fares did not fit in `limit`.

Fares go stale within minutes: a current price comes from a new search, not from an earlier result.

airline_codes.description: Restricts the search to these airline codes, e.g. ["LY"].

departure_date_from.description: First date of a departure range.

departure_date_to.description: Last date of a departure range.

exclude_airline_codes.description: Airline codes left out of the results.

from_airport.description: Origin IATA code, e.g. "TLV". One origin per search; a second one is refused rather than searched.

limit.description: Maximum flights to return, after merging and sorting.

max_price.description: Only flights at or below this price are returned.

max_searches.description: The searches this call may make, up or down. Unset is the normal behaviour: with the caller's own key the cap covers the request when the request is reasonable (a whole month at three trip lengths is 93 combinations and a whole month x 3 nights x 3 destinations is 279; both run in full) and anything past it is sampled evenly across the range rather than cut short. A lower value spends fewer searches on a wide search; a higher one -- to a hard maximum of 300 -- covers a grid wider than that.

max_stops.description: Maximum stops per flight. 0 means non-stop only.

passengers.description: One entry per traveller, not a count: 1 adult, 2 child (aged 2-11), 3 infant on lap, 4 infant in seat, e.g. [1, 1, 2] for two adults and a child. At least one adult, each infant on lap needs its own adult, at most 9. Left out, it means one adult. A counts list [adults, children, infants], e.g. [2, 1, 0], or a bare [2] for two adults, is recognised and converted to codes before the search; a list that is valid as codes is searched as codes.

sort_by.description: "best" (the default) and "price" both order by price, cheapest first; "duration" orders shortest first. Applied across all results.

to_airport.description: Destination airport. One IATA code ("BCN"), several separated by commas ("BCN,LIS,ATH"), or a list (["BCN","LIS","ATH"]) -- every shape is accepted and the destinations are compared in the same search.

use_fallback.description: Default: unset. Switches the search to a second, independent flight data source instead of the usual Google Flights page read. Unset already escalates to that source once, automatically, after a search's retries have failed. true forces it inline on every attempt -- much slower, and it can time out. false disables it entirely, that automatic retry included.

verbose.description: Returns every field the upstream sends on each fare, and every fare that was selected, with no row bound. Off by default: a result carries the best rows by the requested sort_by in a compact shape (dates, destination, airline, stops, duration, price, trip length and the booking link), because a wide search over a month and several destinations otherwise produces a megabyte of JSON that some hosts refuse to put in the conversation at all. When true, it adds the arrival times, the per-leg stop counts, the raw stop details and every row past results_returned; results_total always says how many there were.
